summary: Lets CoAP clients and intermediaries avoid keeping per-request state, by introducing an optional extension for longer token lengths. The extra space lets the needed state be carried in the token itself. It updates RFC 7252 and RFC 8323 to extend the definition of the TKL field.

eli5.summary: Instead of remembering every request you sent, you write the notes on a longer name tag and it comes back with the reply.

questions: what is a stateless coap client
how long can a coap token be
how does a client discover extended token support
subtitle: Longer CoAP tokens let clients and proxies stash request state in the token instead of remembering it.

tldr.problem: A CoAP client normally keeps state for every request in flight so it can handle the response, but constrained nodes would rather not, and tokens are limited to 8 bytes.
tldr.mechanism: The client serializes its request state into the token and the server echoes it back. A new optional extension redefines the TKL field so tokens can be much longer, up to 65804 bytes.
tldr.outcome: Clients and intermediaries can avoid per-request state, at the cost of bigger messages and extra care about integrity, replay and privacy of the serialized state.

today: RFC 8974 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021 that updates RFC 7252 and RFC 8323. The unit metadata shows no later RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Tokens and Per-Request State
sections.content:
In the Constrained Application Protocol (CoAP, RFC 7252), a client makes requests and a server answers. While a request is outstanding, the client usually keeps some state to process the response. CoAP links the two with a token: an opaque byte sequence chosen by the client, sent in the request and returned verbatim in the response.

A client can instead serialize part of its state into the token and recover it from the response, trading larger messages for less stored state. Both CoAP over UDP and CoAP over reliable transports (RFC 8323) limit tokens to 8 bytes, which restricts this. The document therefore adds an optional extension for longer tokens. The two ideas can be used independently.

"Stateless" is used loosely here: such a client still keeps state per server, for token generation, retransmission and congestion control, but not per request.
sections.eli5: A token is a name tag on your question. If the tag is big enough to hold your notes, you do not need to remember anything yourself.

sections.title: The Extended TKL Field
sections.content:
The RFC updates RFC 7252 and RFC 8323 with a new definition of the 4-bit Token Length (TKL) field. Values 0 to 12 give the token length in bytes. The other values are special:

  • 13: an 8-bit unsigned integer precedes the token and gives its length minus 13.
  • 14: a 16-bit integer in network byte order precedes the token and gives its length minus 269.
  • 15: reserved. It MUST NOT be sent and MUST be treated as a message-format error.

This raises the maximum representable token length to 65804 bytes. Implementations may support less; for example, a Class 1 constrained node might handle extended tokens only up to 32 bytes. Over UDP, the Path MTU also limits the practical size, since messages are best kept small enough to avoid IP fragmentation.
sections.eli5: The old name tag could hold 8 letters. A special code on the tag now says that a longer name follows, and how long it is.

sections.title: Discovering Server Support
sections.content:
Servers must support extended lengths, and a client finds out in one of two ways. Where Capabilities and Settings Messages (CSMs) exist, such as CoAP over TCP, the server can send the elective Extended-Token-Length capability option (number 6, a uint, base value 8) to state the longest token it accepts in requests. Values below 8 are ignored and values above 65804 are set to 65804. A request with a longer token than announced MUST be handled as a message-format error. If the token is acceptable but the server cannot handle it now, it SHOULD return 5.03 (Service Unavailable).

Otherwise, as in CoAP over UDP, the client uses trial and error. A server without support rejects an extended TKL as a message-format error. Clients REQUIRE a Confirmable message, since a Confirmable message gets a Reset reply while a Non-confirmable one may be silently ignored. The client should send a request that has no other possible format error, such as a GET with only an If-None-Match option and the longest token it intends to use. A response echoing the token means that length is supported.

Clients SHOULD NOT assume support forever. Absent other information, they should treat it as valid for at least 1800 s and at most 86400 s (1 day), and may use DHCP lease times, Router Advertisements or DNS TTLs. A supporting server that cannot handle a token MUST NOT reject it with a Reset; it SHOULD return 5.03 for a temporary problem or 4.00 (Bad Request) if it never can.

Tokens are hop-by-hop, so discovery must be repeated for every hop that will use extended tokens.
sections.eli5: Before writing a long name tag, you ask the other side if they can read one. If they cannot, they hand your tag back unopened.

sections.title: Stateless Clients
sections.content:
A stateless client puts the needed bytes of its per-request state into the token, and the server returns it verbatim. Servers need no change, so interoperability is not affected. The serialization needs protection, and the RFC lists these measures:

  • The client SHOULD protect the integrity of the serialized state.
  • It SHOULD implement replay protection, for example sequence numbers and a replay window; integrity protection is REQUIRED for this.
  • If timing matters, it SHOULD include freshness information such as a timestamp and reject stale responses.
  • It SHOULD encrypt state that is privacy-sensitive.
  • When the format changes, it SHOULD prevent false interoperability with the old format, for example by changing the integrity key.

A client that depends on extended tokens MUST perform discovery in a stateful way, because a Reset message returns only the Message ID, so a stateless client could not tell what failed. Discovery is OPTIONAL where support is known by other means, as in the Constrained Join Protocol for 6TiSCH networks.

Over UDP, Non-confirmable requests avoid retransmission state, though the client still keeps congestion-control state such as NSTART limits. Responses that fail the integrity or freshness checks are handled as RFC 7252 describes: a piggybacked response has its response part silently discarded, and separate or Non-confirmable responses are rejected.
sections.eli5: If you write notes on the tag, a prankster could swap the tag or show you an old one. So you sign the tag, number it and check the date.

sections.title: Stateless Intermediaries
sections.content:
An intermediary normally stores the client's token and address while it asks the origin server. To avoid that, it can serialize the client information plus its own request state into the token it sends onward. This has drawbacks:

  • Observe: without state it cannot aggregate requests for the same resource, which RFC 7641 requires, nor track whether clients still want notifications. So it MUST NOT include an Observe Option in requests unless it keeps both request state and client information.
  • Block-wise transfers (RFC 7959): the server may not tell blocks from different clients apart, so intermediaries must keep operations separate, for example with the Request-Tag Option.
  • Gateway timeouts: without client information it cannot send the 5.04 (Gateway Timeout) response, so it cannot implement such a timeout.
  • Growing tokens: tokens can grow along a chain of stateless intermediaries, so they SHOULD limit the client information they serialize, for example by limiting accepted token lengths or keeping state locally above a limit.
sections.eli5: A messenger who writes everything on the tag cannot keep track of who is still waiting, or give up on someone after a timeout. And the tag can get longer at every stop.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Large tokens can exhaust memory on constrained nodes, so a server supporting them may suffer denial of service from an on-path attacker or malicious client. Implementations must be prepared for this.

For serialized state, an on-path attacker or rogue server could otherwise return modified or unsolicited state and change the client's internal state, so integrity protection on the token is always recommended. The key is used only by the node that created the state, so the choice of scheme is a local matter. When encrypting, the RFC recommends AES-CCM with a 64-bit tag, plus a sequence number and replay window. Where privacy is not needed, HMAC-SHA-256 with a sequence number and replay window may be used.

The replay window depends on how many requests can be outstanding. With a MAX_TRANSMIT_WAIT of 93 s and one request every 10 s, at most 10 are outstanding, and a 32-bit window would be sufficient. Repeating a nonce under the same key breaks AES-CCM badly, so devices with weak entropy sources need a careful nonce scheme; RFC 8613 Appendix B.1.1 shows a model that avoids excessive flash wear.
sections.eli5: Tags that are too long could fill up a tiny desk, and fake tags could fool you. So seal each tag with a secret stamp that only you know, and never reuse a stamp number.

items.label: 8-bit extension
items.desc: An 8-bit integer precedes the token: length minus 13.

items.label: 16-bit extension
items.desc: A 16-bit integer precedes the token: length minus 269.

items.label: Reserved
items.desc: MUST NOT be sent; processed as a message-format error.
